title: ExVerus: Verus Proof Repair via Counterexample Reasoning
claim: Prior counterexample generation from compiled solver queries yields unknown, meaningless values; source-level translation yields simple, interpretable counterexamples.
layout: 3 columns; buggy code left, ours top-right, prior bottom-right; red/green callouts
description: A dense, code-centric figure. On the left, a task spec box (find max of an array, with pre- and postconditions) sits above a Verus buggy proof listing. One invariant line is highlighted red with an error callout. Two dotted-border horizontal panels sit on the right, each with arrows labeled 'Verification Condition' and 'Solve'. The top panel, with a green check and 'ExVerus CEX Generation', shows a synthesized Z3Py script with green annotations (adaptive variable concretization, semantic preserving, direct source-level translation). It leads to a SAT output with several simple counterexamples. The bottom panel, with a red warning, shows Verus's compiled SMT query. It leads to an 'unknown' result with red warnings about random values and stripped types. Green and red contrast carries the argument.
caption: Motivating example from \verusbench (Misc/findmax) showing advantages of source-level \cex (the \tool \cex generation on top right) v.s. Verus's \cex (Verus \cex generation on button right).
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising results in automating formal verification. However, existing approaches treat proof generation as a static, end-to-end prediction over source code, relying on limited verifier feedback and lacking access to concrete program behaviors. We present EXVERUS, a counterexample-guided framework that enables LLMs to reason about proofs using behavioral feedback via counterexamples. When a proof fails, EXVERUS automatically generates and validates counterexamples, and then guides the LLM to generalize them into inductive invariants to block these failures. Our evaluation shows that EXVERUS significantly improves proof accuracy, robustness, and token efficiency over the state-of-the-art prompting-based Verus proof generator.
